readerTitle: Why the same burger in two cities is the whole product
caseNote: 실제 기업 (McDonald's, 1950~60년대 Ray Kroc의 프랜차이즈 확장) + 가상 사례 (버거 매장 두 곳, 소프트웨어 고객지원팀) · 점수와 시간 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 서비스 품질은 평균이 아니라 편차로 판단한다. 고객은 평균을 경험하지 않고, 자기가 받은 한 번을 경험한다.
misconception: 평균 만족도가 높으면 서비스가 좋은 것이다. 가끔 최고의 경험을 주면 가끔 실망을 줘도 상쇄된다.

sources.text: McDonald's Corporation, company history (Ray Kroc, franchising from 1955, Hamburger University 1961)
Kroc, R. with Anderson, R. (1977). Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald's.
점수 차트와 고객지원 응답 시간은 설명용 가상 수치

factChecks.note: Ray Kroc가 1955년 첫 프랜차이즈 매장을 열었고, 'Quality, Service, Cleanliness and Value(QSC&V)'를 운영 원칙으로 내세웠다는 내용을 McDonald's 공식 역사 자료로 확인하세요.
Hamburger University 개교 연도(1961년, 일리노이주 Elk Grove Village 매장 지하)를 McDonald's 공식 자료로 확인하세요.
차트 계산: 안정적 매장 8+8+7+9+8=40, 평균 8. 들쭉날쭉한 매장 10+9+5+10+6=40, 평균 8. 두 매장 평균이 같다는 점을 다시 확인했습니다.
'나쁜 경험이 좋은 경험보다 더 무겁게 기억된다'는 부정성 편향(negativity bias)을 일반적 경향으로만 서술했습니다. 특정 수치나 연구 결과는 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the same burger in two cities is the whole product
body: A traveler pulls off a highway in a town she has never seen. She picks a restaurant she has never been to.
She isn't taking a risk. She already knows what the fries will taste like. That certainty took decades of hard, unglamorous work to build.

image.label: Two identical burger trays in two different towns
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눠 왼쪽은 사막 도로변, 오른쪽은 눈 내린 마을. 양쪽 테이블에 똑같은 버거·감자튀김 쟁반이 같은 각도로 놓여 있음. 따뜻한 일러스트 스타일. 실제 브랜드 로고, 골든 아치, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Two locations, same average score.
body: You run two burger restaurants. Both average 8 out of 10 in customer ratings.
At the first, almost every visit scores 7 to 9. At the second, ratings swing between 5 and 10. You have budget to improve only one this quarter. Where do you start?

options.feedback: The average hides who got the 5. Those customers may not return, even though the number looks fine.

options.text: The swinging location: find out what causes the bad visits and remove it
options.feedback: You may lose a few 10s, but every customer can now count on a good meal. That promise is what brings people back.

options.text: The steady location: push it to hit 10s like the other one
options.feedback: Raising the ceiling is worth doing later. Right now the second location is quietly losing customers on its bad nights.

cards.title: Same average. Very different customers.
body: Five visits at each location. Both add up to 40, an average of 8.
At the steady location, every guest leaves satisfied. At the other, two of five guests had a poor meal. They don't experience the average. They experience their visit.

cards.title: Service consistency
body: **Service consistency** means customers get the same good experience every time, whatever the day, the shift, the staff member or the location.
A customer isn't buying one meal. They are buying a promise about every future meal. Each visit either confirms the promise or breaks it.
People also tend to remember a bad experience more vividly than a good one. So one poor visit can undo several great ones.

cards.title: Ray Kroc's obsession: the same fries everywhere.
body: When Ray Kroc began franchising McDonald's in the 1950s, he wasn't chasing the best burger in America. He wanted a burger in one town to match the burger in the next.

He summed up the standard as QSC&V: quality, service, cleanliness and value. In 1961 he opened a training school, Hamburger University, so that owners and managers everywhere learned to run restaurants the same way.
The food was simple. **The reliability** was the product.

image.label: A map with identical restaurant pins spreading out
image.brief: 1950~60년대 레트로 포스터 스타일의 미국 지도. 똑같은 작은 식당 아이콘이 점점 퍼져 나가고, 아이콘마다 같은 버거 그림. 실제 McDonald's 로고, 골든 아치, 캐릭터는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Find where the bad visits come from.
body: Bad visits rarely happen at random. They cluster around a few sources:
list: **People:** a new hire on the Saturday rush
**Shifts:** the closing crew skips steps the morning crew follows
**Inputs:** a supplier's product varies week to week
**Peaks:** quality holds at 20 orders an hour and breaks at 60
cards.callout: Track the worst visits, not the average. Then fix the source that produces them.

cards.title: Consistent isn't the same as good.
body: A business can be reliably mediocre. Consistency only helps once the standard itself is worth repeating.

It can also go too far. Rigid scripts make staff sound like machines, and customers notice. The aim is a consistent *outcome*: the order is right, the wait is reasonable, the guest feels looked after. How a skilled person gets there can still flex.
Narrowing the spread may also mean fewer surprise 10s. That trade is usually worth it, but not for every business. A chef's tasting menu sells variety on purpose.

cards.title: Now it's a software support team.
body: Your app's support team answers tickets in 2 hours on average. Customers praise the speed. But one in twenty tickets waits more than three days, usually tricky ones that nobody wants to pick up. Those users often cancel.
What do you do first?

options.text: Hire two more agents to bring the average down to 1 hour
options.feedback: Faster on average, but the tricky tickets may still sit. You'd pay for speed where customers are already happy.

options.text: Set a maximum wait, and route any ticket nearing it to a senior person
options.feedback: This targets the long waits that drive cancellations. The average barely moves, but no user is forgotten for days.

options.text: Offer white-glove support to your biggest accounts only
options.feedback: It protects a few key users while everyone else still risks a three-day wait. The promise stays broken for most customers.

cards.title: Customers don't get your average. They get one visit.
body: Judge service by its worst common experience, not its mean. Shrinking the bad tail often wins more loyalty than adding more peaks.
**Try it today:** look at your last 20 customer interactions. Find the three worst. What did they have in common?
